Don't look for your pre-ordained niche in the world. Carve out your own space. Architectural and homebuilding skills can be particularly empowering and I've long been interested in developing technologies to aid the solitary owner-builder. There's no real reason housing is expensive or more complicated than assembling a piece of Ikea furniture other than that it suits the bankers. Go look at a typical construction site. The built habitat sure as hell isn't built by rocket scientists... I'm keen on the notion of 'proactive futurism'. The best way to predict the future is to make it yourself.

The short-sighted analysis and projections of the future we see in the media are alternately dystopian and utopian depending on who's offering a sales pitch --mostly dystopian as it sells more easily than optimism these days. What I call Caveman Science Fiction. Everything an alegory on hubris that ends in disaster. And there's a lot of futurism that has succumb to a cargo-cult mentality; singularity and space futurism in particular. A vision of the future that, like religion, leaves you hopeful yet powerless. Sitting on the end of the faux runway waiting for Elon Musk's mothership.

But generally, futurism is offering us a cautionary optimism. In many ways life is, and long has been, steadily improving. The individual is becoming more empowered, if only they will pick up and claim the tools scattered around them. We see that if society's outlook is generally dystopian, it's culture is probably looking backward and inward as well. Cultivating willful ignorance to avoid responsibility. Systematically committing what Camus called philosophical suicide. There's a dark utility to dystopianism. The hopeless cannot act. Cannot fight. They can only be victims of the future. They can only be reluctantly shoved backward-facing into it instead of facing it, claiming it as their own, shaping it, and striding into it. And so will leave the driving to someone else.

There was a comedian who did a bit about how his mother conned him as a child into not being so eager to learn to drive a car by making it seem more difficult than it was. When they were in the car, she would continuously fiddle with every button and knob on the dashboard making it seem like driving was such hard and complicated work he would never hope to manage it. So when other kids reached their teens and started pestering their parents for a car of their own, he was happy to just take the bus or ride a bike.

There's plenty of reason to be optimistic about the long-term. We're never going to reach utopia, but the point is in the striving for it. To visualize something better, describe it, and try to make it. To take responsibility for it and not leave the driving to someone else.
